1.pericope_label: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and reigned fifty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Hephzi–bah. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, after the abominations of the heathen, whom the Lord cast out before the children of Israel. For he built up again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; and he reared up altars for Baal, and made a grove, as did Ahab king of Israel; and worshipped all the host of heaven, and served them. And he built altars in the house of the Lord, of which the Lord said, In Jerusalem will I put my name. And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord. And he made his son pass through the fire, and observed times, and used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the Lord, to provoke him to anger. And he set a graven image of the grove that he had made in the house, of which the Lord said to David, and to Solomon his son, In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all tribes of Israel, will I put my name for ever: Neither will I make the feet of Israel move any more out of the land which I gave their fathers; only if they will observe to do according to all that I have commanded them, and according to all the law that my servant Moses commanded them. But they hearkened not: and Manasseh seduced them to do more evil than did the nations whom the Lord destroyed before the children of Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott allows that the early accession may help to account for Manasseh's deviation from his father's religious policy, though he denies that it is necessary to assume with Thenius a regency by the queen-mother, since Manasseh may have been older than his years. He alone supplies the imperial setting, that Manasseh was a tributary first to Esar-haddon and then to Assurbanipal on the authority of the Assyrian inscriptions, that his name and his successor's suggest Egyptian influence, and that combinations with Egypt against Assyria were popular at that epoch, so that the religious revolution sits inside a foreign policy rather than beside it; he notes too that the Babylonian astrology had been introduced under Ahaz, so Manasseh was reviving rather than inventing. He is exact about the altars, the general notice meaning the two courts and the particular one including even the inner court where sacrifice was offered to Jehovah, places the image of the Asherah within the temple itself and probably in the holy place as the climax of the impiety, and gives the reason the comparison with the dispossessed nations is so damning: they worshipped only their own national gods, whereas Judah forsook its own God and was ready to adopt almost any foreign worship it met.

Clarke says everyone may see that the word our version renders grove must signify an idol and not a grove, and identifies it with the Babylonian and Roman goddess known under other names; he itemises the divinations of the same verse, observing times meaning divination by the clouds, by their course and kinds and contrary directions, enchantments meaning incantations and spells and charms, dealing with familiar spirits meaning a necromancer and raiser of spirits, and the wizards being the knowing ones.

Henry grants the same influence of youth and then refuses it as any excuse, on a comparison that settles the matter: Manasseh's coming to the crown so young may help to account for the apostasy and yet will by no means excuse him, for his grandson Josiah came to it younger still and acted well. He specifies two effects of the youth, that Manasseh was puffed up with his honour and thought himself wise because he was great, valuing himself on undoing what his father had done, it being too common for novices to be lifted up with pride; and that he was easily wrought upon by seducers who lay in wait, the enemies of Hezekiah's reformation flattering him, gaining his ear and using his power at their pleasure. He adds the grim arithmetic that this was the only very bad reign in Judah that was also a long one.

debates: Whether Manasseh's youth excuses any of the apostasy, where Ellicott allows it as explanation while denying a regency was needed, and Henry allows the explanation but refuses the excuse outright, since Josiah came to the throne younger still and acted well.

Whether the word rendered grove means a grove or an idol, which Clarke and Ellicott agree means an idol, Clarke identifying it with a known goddess and Ellicott placing the image inside the temple itself.

Why Judah's idolatry was reckoned worse than the Canaanites', which Ellicott answers by distinguishing a people who kept to their own national gods from one that forsook its God and would adopt almost any foreign worship it met.
outliers: Ellicott reports from the Assyrian inscriptions that Manasseh paid tribute successively to Esar-haddon and Assurbanipal, which places the reign inside an imperial as well as a religious history.
Henry observes that this was the only very bad reign in Judah that was also a long one, fifty-five years, longer than any other king's.

10.pericope_label: And the Lord spake by his servants the prophets, saying, Because Manasseh king of Judah hath done these abominations, and hath done wickedly above all that the Amorites did, which were before him, and hath made Judah also to sin with his idols: Therefore thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Behold, I am bringing such evil upon Jerusalem and Judah, that whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle. And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down. And I will forsake the remnant of mine inheritance, and deliver them into the hand of their enemies; and they shall become a prey and a spoil to all their enemies; Because they have done that which was evil in my sight, and have provoked me to anger, since the day their fathers came forth out of Egypt, even unto this day. Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another; beside his sin wherewith he made Judah to sin, in doing that which was evil in the sight of the Lord. Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and all that he did, and his sin that he sinned, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? And Manasseh slept with his fathers, and was buried in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza: and Amon his son reigned in his stead.

schools.summary: Ellicott works carefully through the question of which prophets spoke, holding that the general expression is used because the historian found no name in his source, that Isaiah may still have been living but that the protests were more probably his disciples' since the style is not his, and weighing Ewald's proposal that the passage is an extract from the lost work the chronicler cites for the words of the seers who spoke to Manasseh, before judging it much more likely to be a summary of many such addresses. He reads the measuring line and plummet architecturally, as suggesting Jerusalem levelled and laid even with the ground by the same rigorous rule already used on Samaria, and takes the wiping of the dish for the destruction of the people and the turning of it for the overthrow of the city, allowing with Thenius that the two together may mean simply making an end. He identifies the innocent blood as the prophets' and their followers', quotes an account of why the reaction came, and records that the chronicler's story of Manasseh's captivity and repentance is now allowed by the best critics to be genuine history though once dismissed as an edifying fiction.

Clarke takes both measures of the sentence dynastically, that Jerusalem will be treated as Samaria was and that since the house of Ahab was destroyed with not a man of his race left to sit on the throne of Israel, so the royal family of Judah shall be destroyed with none of their race to sit on the throne, nor shall Judah have a throne to sit on; and on the wiped dish he finds an entirely different image by way of the Latin, which has God blotting out Jerusalem as tablets are blotted out, a metaphor from writing with a stile on boards spread with wax, one end sharp for tracing and the other blunt for rubbing out.

Henry does not ask who spoke but why, setting out the prophetic office in three stages: the prophets were sent first to teach the knowledge of God, then, if that failed, to reprove men that they might repent, and if that failed too, to foretell the judgments of God, either that the terror might awaken those whom his love could not or that the execution might demonstrate the divine mission of those who foretold it; the prophets, he concludes, were deputed judges to those who would not receive them as teachers. On the indictment he reads a double count, that Manasseh had done wickedly though he knew better and had debauched the people of God whom he taught and forced to sin, and that besides all that he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, multiplying his murders in every corner and filling the measure of its blood-guiltiness to the brim.

debates: Which prophets delivered the sentence, where Ellicott rules out Isaiah on grounds of style, weighs and rejects Ewald's view that the passage is an authentic contemporary oracle, and settles for a summary of many prophetic addresses.

What the measuring line and plummet signify, which Clarke reads dynastically as the extinction of the royal house on the pattern of Ahab's, and Ellicott architecturally as the city levelled to the ground.
What the wiped dish means, where Ellicott divides the wiping from the turning as people and city, while Clarke follows the Latin into an entirely different image of a wax tablet rubbed smooth.
outliers: Ellicott records a reversal of scholarly opinion, that the chronicler's account of Manasseh's captivity and repentance is now allowed by the best critics to be genuine history though it was once the fashion to call it an edifying fiction.
Henry sets out the prophetic office in three stages and concludes that the prophets were deputed judges to those who would not receive them as teachers.

19.pericope_label: Amon was twenty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, as his father Manasseh did. And he walked in all the way that his father walked in, and served the idols that his father served, and worshipped them: And he forsook the Lord God of his fathers, and walked not in the way of the Lord. And the servants of Amon conspired against him, and slew the king in his own house. And the people of the land slew all them that had conspired against king Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his stead. Now the rest of the acts of Amon which he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? And he was buried in his sepulchre in the garden of Uzza: and Josiah his son reigned in his stead.

schools.summary: Ellicott adds the detail that the name Amon is perhaps that of the Egyptian sun-god, which suits an idolatrous father, and takes the servants who conspired, on the common use of the phrase, for courtiers or palace officials, saying plainly that nothing further is known of the circumstances of the murder.

Clarke reports the rabbinical remark, which he thinks not wholly without foundation, that the sons of idolatrous kings who succeeded their fathers seldom reigned more than two years, and gives four instances; he will not guess at the motive for the murder, saying we cannot tell what reason the servants had, but infers from the sequel that it was not a popular act since the people of the land rose and slew the regicides; and he judges the reign in one line, that we hear enough of this man when we hear he was as bad as his father was at first but did not copy his father's repentance. He then closes the chapter with a sustained philological argument that the word rendered grove means an idol, assembling Jarchi, who makes it a tree worshipped by the Gentiles as the oak was worshipped by the ancient Druids in Britain, Castel's lexicon, which defines it as a wooden image dedicated to Astarte or Venus, Theodoret, cited as identifying the Greek word with Astarte and Venus, and the Targum of Ben Uzziel, which renders the command as cutting down the oaks of their adoration; and he clinches it from the next chapter, where Josiah brings the grove out of the house of the Lord, asking what grove there could have been in the temple when none was planted there and there was no room for any.

Henry asks why the successor was a son born when Manasseh was forty-five and offers two possibilities, that Manasseh had sacrificed his other sons in his zeal for his idols or that having been dedicated to those idols they were refused by the people. He reads the three charges against Amon as a single renunciation, since he forsook the God of his fathers, disobeyed the commands given them and disclaimed their covenant, and from it draws the warning that those who set bad examples, though they may repent themselves, cannot be sure that those whom they have drawn into sin will repent. On the murder he makes the symmetry explicit, that the servants who should have guarded him murdered him and the house which should have been his castle of defence became the place of his execution, so that having profaned God's house with his idols he had his own polluted with his blood, and however unrighteous the doers were, God was righteous who suffered it.

debates: Why Amon reigned only two years, where Clarke finds a rabbinical pattern holding for the sons of idolatrous kings and gives four instances, while Henry and Ellicott treat the brevity as the accident of a palace murder.

Whether the word rendered grove can mean a grove at all, which Clarke settles against the English by assembling four authorities and then by asking what grove could have stood inside the temple that Josiah cleared.

How the murder should be read, which Henry takes as exact retribution on a king who had profaned God's house, while Clarke and Ellicott both decline to assign a motive and note that nothing further is known.
outliers: Clarke quotes Jarchi that the word means a tree worshipped by the Gentiles, as the oak was worshipped by the ancient Druids in Britain.
Henry notes that the people by their representatives did justice on the traitors and put them to death, since though Amon was a bad king he was their king.
